support_summary: D1: four cardiology topics in a 2x2 maturity/specificity quadrant design with standardized prompts, but all within cardiac resynchronization therapy and author-defined with no sampling frame; D2: example prompts in Table 1 and remaining prompts in Supplementary Table S2, 'ChatGPT-5 was queried using the GPT-5 model', tools accessed 'through their publicly available web interfaces (free tier) between August 2025 and January 2026'; D3: 'no advanced, paid, or custom configuration (e.g. temperature, custom instructions) was applied', history cleared and cross-session memory inactive, each prompt submitted once, but no retry rule stated; D4: references 'manually verified by the investigators to confirm bibliographic accuracy (publication title, authors, journal, year of publication, DOI...)', hallucination required failure of 'DOI and title searches', but the verification databases are not named; D5: bibliographic verification was by the investigators who ran the study, with independence/blinding stated only for the three experts rating relevance, and no vendor role reported; D6: 'three experts assessed this corpus independently and asynchronously, blinded to the originating tool or source' with Fleiss kappa for relevance/key-reference ratings, but duplicate verification of bibliographic accuracy is not stated; D7: methods rule that citations with 'minor bibliographic discrepancies' whose source 'could nonetheless be reliably identified' were 'not classified as hallucinations' while untraceable citations were, but minor-discrepancy counts are not given apart (only 0 hallucinated in main analysis and 10 (17%) in the subanalysis); D8: all five tools, four topics and the 'pre-specified subanalysis' are reported with supplementary material, but no registration or protocol is cited to check against.

D1: 10 clinician questions 'sourced directly from clinical guidelines published by the North American Spine Society' plus 10 author-written patient mirrors of the same topics, a single narrow field with no random sampling; D2: both persona prompts printed word for word and versions given for ChatGPT 5.0, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and OpenEvidence 2.7.12 with 'All queries were performed in October 2025' on default web interfaces, but Microsoft Copilot has no version; D3: 'User-adjustable hyperparameters (e.g., temperature) were not uniformly available... and were not recorded', internet search enabled and a new session per question, with a stated reprompt only when more than 5 citations were returned; D4: 'manually verified by the authors using PubMed and publisher websites to confirm its existence and the accuracy of its metadata (authors, title, year, journal, PMID/DOI)', fabricated defined as no record 'in any database'; D5: verification was by the author team, described as 'Three independent medical student reviewers performed the citations verification', with their separation from prompt generation not stated and no vendor role reported; D6: three independent reviewers, 'Inter-rater reliability was high (percent agreement 95.4%, Cohen's kappa = 0.918)' and discordant scores 'resolved by consensus with the senior author'; D7: methods rubric score 2 accurate / score 1 'real, verifiable article, but contained one or more errors in its metadata' / score 0 fabricated, with counts for all three given per model in Table 3; D8: all five models and both prompt types are reported with counts, but no registration, protocol or preprint is cited.

D1: prompts built from all 19 recommendations of one guideline, the AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults, in three engineered perspectives, a named frame but a single narrow topic set chosen by the authors; D2: model named as 'ChatGPT (Version 4o mini, free public version, OpenAI)' and prompts submitted 'between October and November of 2024', but the engineered prompt wording itself is not printed word for word, only the standard follow-up request for references is described; D3: no generation settings (temperature, browsing or system configuration) are reported at all, only a 'newly opened private browsing window' per prompt pair and asynchronous submission; D4: 'A fabricated reference was defined as a reference cited by ChatGPT but not indexed in PubMed' - fabrication rested on a single source, PubMed, with inaccuracies checked against PubMed records for title, authors, journal, year, pages, volume and PMID; D5: the same 4 medical student graders who 'submitted prompts to ChatGPT independently and asynchronously' also graded the responses, with the senior author facilitating the Delphi process, and no vendor role reported; D6: 'Responses were independently assessed by 4 medical student graders using the rubric', including the reference domains, but no agreement figure or blinding for the citation grading is reported; D7: methods definitions separate fabricated references from 'inaccuracies... with regard to title, authors, journal, publication year, page number, volume, and PMID', with fabricated counts and per-field inaccuracy counts reported apart in Table III; D8: all 19 recommendations, three perspectives and recommendation-strength strata are reported in Tables I-III and supplements, but no registration or protocol is cited. Overall high on D4.

D1: 14 author-designed questions on one topic (midshaft clavicle fractures), patient questions shaped by Google Trends searches for 'broken collarbone'/'clavicle fracture' and clinical scenarios written by the authors, with the full list printed in Table 1; D2: all 14 prompts printed word for word in Table 1, 'On August 31, 2024, ChatGPT-4o mini was prompted', with separate chat sessions stated; D3: no generation settings are reported - nothing on temperature, system instructions or browsing - though each question was submitted three times on the same day and all 42 responses were graded; D4: 'verified through independent searches conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus, including searches of article titles, abstracts, keywords, and authors'; D5: outputs 'independently evaluated by two orthopaedic registrars (CK and RC) and two senior orthopaedic surgeons (MS and BS)', i.e. the author team, with no stated separation from the generation step and no vendor role; D6: four independent evaluators with 'discrepancies in grading resolved through discussion until a consensus was reached', but no numeric agreement figure for the reference verification is reported; D7: methods rule - references 'classified as incorrect if they could be located but contained inaccuracies (such as errors in the title, authors, publication date, or journal), or fabricated if they could not be located at all', with counts reported apart (1 correct, 14 incorrect, 113 fabricated of 128); D8: all 14 questions and all three repeats are reported in Table 2 for the single model, but no registration or protocol is cited.

D1: eight author-designed questions on one topic (Achilles tendon ruptures), patient questions derived from Google Trends searches for 'ruptured Achilles tendon'/'torn Achilles tendon' and clinical scenarios written by the authors, full list in Table 1; D2: all eight prompts printed word for word in Table 1, 'ChatGPT 3.5 was presented with a series of eight questions' and 'Each question was entered twice on February 6, 2024' as a distinct 'New Chat'; D3: no generation settings are reported - nothing on temperature, system instructions or browsing - though both runs of every question were assessed; D4: 'The accuracy of the references... was verified by conducting searches across MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus'; D5: responses 'independently evaluated... by two orthopaedic registrars (CK and RC) and two senior orthopaedic surgeons (MS and BS)', the author team, with no stated separation from generation and no vendor role; D6: four independent evaluators with discrepancies 'discussed until a consensus was reached', but no numeric agreement figure for reference verification is reported; D7: references 'deemed incorrect if they contained inaccurate details such as the title, authors, date of publication, or journal information or were considered fabricated if the reference could not be found', with counts reported apart (16 correct, 19 incorrect, 12 fabricated of 47); D8: all eight questions and both repeats are reported in Table 2 for the single model, but no registration or protocol is cited.

D1: 47 medications assembled from a named frame - FDA-approved migraine preventives plus the AAN 2012 guideline categories plus five pre-specified negative-control medications with no migraine role - spanning all evidence grades; D2: the prompt is printed verbatim ('is [medication] an effective medication for the prevention of migraine? Give 3 citations if they exist'), 'OpenAI's ChatGPT-3.5 was utilized with a new chat session and previous chat history cleared' and queries run 'on April 14, 2023 and April 16, 2023', with the full transcript in Supplemental Material S1; D3: no generation settings are reported at all, only that one author (LSM) queried each medication once and 'This methodology was determined prior to the initiation of any queries'; D4: citation 'titles searched on both Google Scholar and PubMed to determine if they were real literature or hallucinations' - two sources, but the methods describe the check as a title search while outcomes also count correctly cited papers; D5: generation was by one named author and no separate verifier is identified, the same small team doing every step with no separation stated and no vendor role; D6: no duplicate or blinded verification and no agreement figure is reported anywhere - verification appears single and unblinded while real-versus-hallucinated calls required judgement; D7: three categories are reported with separate counts - 33/115 'real papers that were correctly cited', 76/115 'hallucinations', and 6/115 papers that 'had the names of real papers but the citation details... were new creations' (Table 2 gives per-paper error detail); D8: all 47 medications are reported with citation counts in Table 1 and the method was fixed before querying, but there is no registration or preprint to check against. Overall high on D6.

D1: 20 author-developed questions from 'the most frequently encountered patient presentations' at one restorative dentistry clinic plus textbooks and exam banks, filtered by a Lawshe content-validity threshold (CVR >= 0.62 from 10 experts) - a stated selection process but an author-picked single-field set; D2: exact versions and access points are listed (ChatGPT-5 via chat.openai.com, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini 3 Flash), 'All models were accessed on December 25, 2025, through their free-tier web interfaces' and the diagnostic question is quoted verbatim, but the follow-up prompt requesting references is described rather than quoted; D3: 'All models were accessed through their standard web-based interfaces using default settings; therefore, temperature and other generation parameters were not manually adjustable', web browsing enabled for all, history disabled, 'Each case was queried only once per model, and no response regeneration was performed'; D4: 'All references were searched in the PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science databases' and fabricated meant 'could not be retrieved from any database'; D5: 'Reference assessments were conducted independently by both study authors' - the authors also prepared and submitted the prompts, so generation and verification overlap, with no vendor role; D6: both authors assessed independently with 'consensus reached through joint evaluation in cases of disagreement', but no agreement figure for the reference classification is reported (the ICC reported covers the 42 specialists' Likert ratings) and assessors were not blinded to model; D7: four categories defined in the methods ('accurate and relevant', 'partially accurate', 'misleading/irrelevant', 'fabricated') with per-model counts for each category in Table 3; D8: all five models and all 20 questions are reported including the reference table, with ethics approval (2025/288) stated but no registration or protocol cited.

D1: a 40-question bank 'based on literature and clinical consultation experience', from which 'The top 10 most concerned questions selected by cohort A were used for subsequent LLM evaluation' - caregiver-concern selection within a single condition (hypospadias), not a random or framed sample; D2: 'The complete LLM access protocol (URLs, model versions, browser environment, session management, configuration parameters, and the full Chinese/English prompt set) is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1', free-tier web interfaces, 'All conclusions are time-stamped to April 6, 2025'; D3: free-tier interfaces 'without paid functions or customized settings', Chrome 'with cleared cookies and cache', 'each question submitted as an independent single-turn query in a separate conversation window using a standardized... template', and boilerplate uniformly removed across models, but no regeneration/retry rule is stated; D4: verification by 'a standardized search hierarchy (PubMed - CrossRef DOI resolver - Google Scholar - CNKI)' covering existence and bibliographic detail, with DOI resolution tested directly; D5: 'Reference authenticity was independently verified by 2 trained reviewers (XH and WH)', reviewers distinct from the researchers (TK and CY) who built and stratified the question bank, and no vendor role is reported; D6: two independent reviewers with 'Cohen kappa = 0.702 preadjudication' ('raw agreement 80.9%... across 157 paired records') and discrepancies 'resolved by reapplying the V/PV/F/G/NR framework against canonical sources'; D7: the 5-category V/PV/F/G/NR scheme is defined in the methods (V verifiable, PV partially verifiable, F fabricated, G guideline-based/nonspecific, NR no references), applied conservatively ('unretrievable articles were strictly coded as Fabricated'), with per-model counts for every category in Table 2; D8: all five models and all 10 questions are reported including the full citation classification in Table 2 and appendices, but no registration is cited.

D1: questions 'manually collected by the authors from Reddit' (all posts on the Hot pages of r/Keloids, r/SCAR and r/PlasticSurgery as of April 6, 2025, with keyword Scar/Keloid) plus 49 questions from 3 medical websites - a stated frame, but a popularity-based Hot-page sample with exclusions and first classification by one author (MR); D2: the model is named only as 'GPT-4' (also 'ChatGPT-4'), with no exact version or release string, no generation date (only the April 6, 2025 question-collection date), and no interface stated, although 'no specialized prompt instructions were appended to the question inputs'; D3: no generation settings are reported - only 'a new chat session was initiated for each question'; D4: 'Each reference was verified through direct links or a Google search' - no bibliographic database is named, a single general search engine carrying the real-versus-fabricated call (Multimedia Appendix 4 tool); D5: the paper does not state who performed the reference evaluation, so verifier separation from generation cannot be judged (the three plastic surgeons are named only for the NLAT-AI content scoring); D6: no duplicate, blinded or agreement-checked reference verification is described (ICCs reported cover the PEMAT-AI/DISCERN-AI/GQS/NLAT-AI content tools, not reference checking); D7: no partial-match rule is stated - results are a simple dichotomy of 2867/3250 'actual sources (actual websites or academic papers)' versus 383 hallucinated references, so real but miscited sources are folded into 'actual' with no separate count; D8: all 16 Reddit question groups and the website-question set are reported with appendices, for the single model, but no registration or protocol is cited. Overall high on D2, D4 and D7.

D1: nine topics listed in Table 1, deliberately balanced as three Researched, three Controversial and three Open topics under stated classification criteria, with a three-expert panel classifying by consensus - a design that balances difficulty levels, though the topics themselves were author-identified; D2: the standardized prompt is quoted verbatim ('Write a 1,500-word literature review on the topic...'), models are named (GPT-4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-3, DeepSeek R1) with free/basic access routes described, but no generation date or period is stated anywhere; D3: no generation settings are reported at all - nothing on temperature, browsing or system instructions, nor on repeats, output selection or retries; D4: references 'manually retrieved and verified through academic databases such as PubMed and Google Scholar' - two sources named non-exhaustively, with the fields actually checked and any DOI testing not described; D5: the paper does not state who verified the references (the seven ophthalmologists are described as scoring review quality, accuracy, bias and relevance), so verifier independence cannot be judged; D6: no duplicate or blinded reference verification and no agreement figure for it is described - the ICC reported covers the expert review scores only; D7: scoring categories are stated in the analysis ('True and relevant = 1; True but not relevant = 0; Fictitious (hallucination) = -1') with per-model category percentages in Table 2, but no rule is given for references with wrong bibliographic fields on a real paper; D8: all four models and all nine topics are reported in Tables 2-4, but no registration, protocol or preprint is cited. Overall high: D3, D5 and D6 at no information together leave the citation verification unchecked.

D1: 'We collected all oral and maxillofacial surgery multiple-choice questions from the CNMLE (dentistry category) between 2013 and 2024, totaling 110 questions' - a complete examination frame, with image questions removed for a stated fairness reason (unimodal open-source models); D2: models named as Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-0528, ChatGPT o3-pro, Gemini 2.5 pro and Claude 4.0, entered 'on June 5, 2025' under a standardized protocol with session isolation described, but the 110 question prompts themselves are not printed and Qwen3 carries no version detail; D3: 'Generation parameters were fixed for open-source models (Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1-0528: temperature = 0.7, top_k = 40, top_p = 0.9 [default]); proprietary models used default configurations', each query in a new session, with failed queries 'put on hold' - the failure rule is vague; D4: 'Chinese references were verified using databases including CNKI and Wanfang, while English references were searched in PubMed..., Web of Science... and Google Scholar', but 'verified' required only being located and 'pertinent to the query content', with no field-level accuracy or DOI check; D5: one researcher entered the questions and 'two other researchers immediately evaluated the responses', but who searched the references is not stated, so separation for the citation check is unclear, with no vendor role; D6: no duplicate, blinded or agreement-checked reference verification is described; D7: references 'located within these databases and pertinent to the query content were classified as verified, those unavailable or irrelevant were classified as unverified' - real but irrelevant references and nonexistent references are merged in one category (labelled 'Fabricated' in Table 5) with no way to re-cut the counts; D8: all five models are reported by question type, disease category and reference authenticity (Table 5), but no registration or protocol is cited.

D1: only two author-developed prompts/topics (Teach-Back at discharge; neutropenic diet and sepsis/length of stay), printed in full, with no topic sampling frame; D2: 'Terminology was not established in advance, and participants reported chatbot versions inconsistently' - of 7 ChatGPT users only a minority named a version, Claude/Copilot/Gemini/OpenEvidence/Perplexity versions mostly 'free' or unspecified, though session dates (Aug. 21 and Sept. 18, 2024) are given; D3: settings varied within arms - Copilot prompters variously used 'Creative' and 'Balanced' modes, 4-7 librarians tested each tool 'depending on availability and access', and OpenEvidence allowed only three interactions against four for other tools (its fourth value imputed in the ANOVA); D4: 'Researchers attempted to verify each unique citation... by searching PubMed, the journal if listed, and via web search', covering existence plus a correct/partially correct distinction, with no DOI testing described; D5: the 13 participating librarians both submitted prompts and took part in verification, with no stated separation between prompters and citation verifiers and no vendor role; D6: duplicate checking is described only for relevance ('reviewed... by two researchers; a third was tie-breaker'), not for the hallucination verification, and no agreement figure is reported; D7: methods rule that 'real' included citations scored 'correct' or 'partially correct' ('mostly matching an existing source, but some missing/incorrect information, i.e. publication date or volume number'), with partial cases folded into 'real' and not counted apart; D8: all six tools and both prompts are reported with real/hallucinated tallies, and the OpenEvidence imputation is disclosed, but no registration or protocol is cited. Overall high on D2.

D1: 20 real-life clinical dilemmas chosen by purposive sampling - physicians in four domains 'selected by each physician independently' for complexity, up to five queries each, with general and diagnosis-only queries excluded by stated criteria; D2: models named with versions (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, Claude Sonnet 3.5) 'accessed using the standard web interfaces' and the full query list is in Supplement Table 3 with examples in the text, but no generation date or period is stated and there was no standardized prompt template (physicians submitted their own queries after a brief training session); D3: 'The physicians also determined the stopping point for their investigation' and 'The median number of iterations clinicians used before truncating attempts to achieve a report with the LLMs was 3 (IQR [2.00, 9.00])' - generation was repeated until the user was satisfied, so the evaluated output was satisfaction-selected; D4: 'The existence of each source was verified through PubMed and Google Scholar searches or through a direct URL search for website sources' and 'Citation accuracy was verified by reviewing the full text of the cited papers', though bibliographic field-by-field accuracy is not described; D5: 'The quality of the reports was evaluated post-hoc by an independent researcher blinded to the source of the reports and to physician satisfaction', with no vendor role; D6: that post-hoc verification was blinded to report source, satisfying the blinded-verification route, though it was a single researcher with no duplicate check or agreement figure; D7: hallucinated, unfaithful and irrelevant citations are defined (Supplement B/C) and reported as separate proportions, with faithfulness calculated from non-hallucinated and relevance from faithful citations, but bibliographic partial matches (real paper, wrong metadata) have no category; D8: exclusions are reported with reasons (27 queries selected, 5 unrelated and 2 diagnostic excluded, 4 Gemini reports 'not captured due to a technical malfunction'), all three models are compared, the study is STROBE-reported with an IRB-approved protocol, but no registration is cited. Overall high on D3.

D1: two author-selected topics only (chronic rhinosinusitis and infantile subglottic hemangioma), with human comparators chosen for 'methodological rigor, clinical relevance, and PRISMA-ScR adherence', and no topic frame; D2: section-by-section prompt templates are printed in Table 1, models are named as ChatGPT-4.0 and Gemini 2.0, generated 'in April 2025 via paid platforms' through 'their standard conversational interfaces'; D3: 'No retrieval augmentation or plugins were used' and browsing/deep-research features were 'not enabled', outputs 'not manually edited', each review generated in triplicate in fresh sessions with 'The first chronologically generated iteration selected for blinded expert evaluation', but numeric settings such as temperature are not reported; D4: 'All references from AI-authored manuscripts were manually verified against PubMed and journal websites' using 'exact title and author matching', with categories covering authors, title, journal, year and pagination; D5: the audit is described as 'an independent post hoc audit', but who performed it is not identified and the author team generated the manuscripts, so separation is only partly established, with no vendor role; D6: the paper gives no information on how many verifiers performed the reference audit, whether they worked apart or blinded, or any agreement figure (the ICCs reported cover the seven-reviewer panel's Likert ratings, not the audit); D7: four categories are defined - '(1) fully accurate...; (2) minor metadata discrepancy...; (3) duplicate citation...; or (4) fabricated or corrupted' - with per-model counts for each (e.g. GPT-4.0 89.6% fully accurate, 9.1% minor errors, 1.3% duplicates, 0% fabricated), but the audit and its rule were post hoc rather than pre-specified; D8: all 10 manuscripts (both models, both topics, both styles) plus the triplicate reproducibility generations are reported, but the citation audit itself was a post hoc addition and no registration or protocol is cited.

D1: queries built from the 12 AAOS glenohumeral arthritis recommendations of 'strong' or 'moderate' strength, with limited/consensus recommendations excluded for lower evidence - a named frame that favours settled, well-evidenced topics - and every query printed in Table I; D2: models named exactly (ChatGPT 'model GPT-4o', Gemini 'model Gemini 2.5 Pro'), 'submitted... on the same day (April 30, 2025)', with all query phrasings printed in Table I, though the interface is not stated; D3: no generation settings are reported - only that 'Each query was submitted only once' with no training or fine-tuning; an extra follow-up (asking ChatGPT for a link) was applied to one arm only, in the results; D4: no verification source is named anywhere for the reference checks - Tables III and IV record only whether a 'Study [was] able to be found' with DOIs/PMIDs, and the methods do not describe reference verification at all; D5: who checked the references is not stated - the two named independent reviewers (S.M.O. and S.B.P) are described only as classifying response concordance with the guideline; D6: duplicate independent review with a third tiebreaker and 'Cohen's kappa coefficient was 0.84' covers the agree/neutral/disagree concordance classification, but duplicate or blinded checking of the references themselves is not described; D7: no rule for reference handling appears in the methods; results nevertheless count cases apart - ChatGPT 3 of 6 references nonexistent and 1 with the wrong journal, Gemini 5 of 32 'inappropriately cited' (Tables III and IV); D8: all 12 recommendations and both models are reported in Tables I and II, but there is no registration or protocol, and the reference analysis appears in results without a methods basis. Overall high: D3, D4 and D5 at no information together leave the citation verification unchecked.

D1: 'A total of 21 nephrology-related questions and 3 renal biopsy reports were curated by experienced nephrologists to reflect common inquiries', balanced 7/7/7 across dialysis, kidney examination and general categories and printed in Table 1, but an author-curated set with no sampling frame (biopsy reports were fictitious constructions); D2: models named (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.0 Ultra, PaLM 2 via Bard, with Bard's PaLM 2 basis explained), accessed 'through their respective official graphical user interfaces... No APIs', with evaluation periods stated (Dec 8-12, 2023, and Oct 21-23, 2024 for GPT-4o - a different period from the other arms), but the reference-request prompt to the top model is not described; D3: questions 'entered individually and repeated three times consecutively', 'all responses... recorded without applying any filtering criteria', GUI use with no settings (temperature, modes) reported; D4: 'an IT engineer was responsible for verifying the accuracy of the references... The verification focused solely on the existence of these sources' - and no database or other verification source is named; D5: verification was assigned to an IT engineer while 'a team of IT engineers queried the AI models', so the verifier came from the generation team, with no vendor role reported; D6: a single engineer performed the verification (Nov 5-10, 2024), with no duplicate check, blinding or agreement figure for it - the double-blind design covered the nephrologist raters of responses, not reference checking; D7: no partial-match rule exists - verification 'focused solely on the existence of these sources, without assessing if the content... directly correlated', so a real title with wrong details counts simply as existing and no partial counts are possible; D8: references were requested only from 'the model with the highest overall ratings' after evaluation ('This model was then asked to provide references for each question'), so the other three models have no citation outcome reported and the reported arm was chosen on its results. Overall high on D6, D7 and D8.

D1: 45 gout nursing questions collected from online search platforms, 10 purposively sampled patients and 15 nurses, coded by two researchers with a third resolving conflicts, then '15 of the most pressing questions were selected' - a subjective selection with no sampling frame, questions listed in Table 1; D2: DeepSeek-R1 via its official web platform (Chrome 126.0.6478.126) and ChatGPT-4.0 via 'the OpenAI official API using Python 3.9.7' - different interfaces by arm, both stated - the unified system prompt is printed in full and 'All queries were submitted between 08:00 and 12:00 (GMT+8) on 20 August 2025', but 'ChatGPT-4.0'/'DeepSeek-R1' carry no release-level version detail; D3: parameter settings are reported in detail ('temperature was set to 0.7... top_p was set to 0.95... maximum output length was limited to 2,048 tokens'), stochastic sampling on, 'Internet browsing was activated for both models' (DeepSeek Browser plugin vs Browse with Bing), citation tools enabled and an 'identical, fixed prompt', but no repeat, selection or retry rule is stated; D4: sources were 'manually searched... to ensure the authenticity of the data materials', but no database or bibliographic source used for that search is named anywhere; D5: who performed the source verification is not stated (the named chief physician and chief nurse evaluated answer accuracy with mDISCERN on de-identified texts, not the source checks); D6: no duplicate, blinded or agreement-checked source verification is described; D7: no partial-match rule is stated - the analysis proceeds by 'eliminating false information, we derived the authentic reference materials', a false-versus-authentic dichotomy with source-type counts only and no count of real-but-miscited references; D8: both models and all 15 questions are reported including source-category and timeliness analyses, with ethics approval (2024-KY-KZ-285-01) stated but no registration or protocol cited. Overall high on D7.

D1: ten author-curated tasks (five essays, five evidence-based Q&A) listed in Table 1, with 'ChatGPT used solely for initial topic pool generation; final topic selection and refinement was performed independently by the authors' and all topics described as 'well-established neuroradiology subject areas', favouring settled areas; D2: both models accessed 'via their respective public web interfaces (DeepSeek-R1, version R1 released January 2025, chat.deepseek.com; ChatGPT-o1, version o1 released December 2024, chat.openai.com) on 18 February 2025', with example prompts printed verbatim and 'The complete set of all ten prompts is provided in Supplementary Text 1 and 2'; D3: 'Parameters such as temperature, top-p, and system prompts were not user-configurable and remained at providers' default settings', 'identical phrasing as standalone queries in fresh chat sessions, with the cache cleared between queries', one output per model-task (20 outputs), with no retry rule stated; D4: references classified 'using PubMed and Google Scholar as the gold standard', with unverifiable defined as 'not locatable via PubMed, Google Scholar, or DOI lookup' - DOI resolution tested directly; D5: outputs were rated by two radiologists (J.N. and S.E.) who are also the authors who selected the topics and built the evaluation framework 'a priori', so verification and study design overlap, with no vendor role; D6: the two radiologists 'blind-scored independently' de-identified, randomized outputs (blinding key held by a non-rating co-author), but no agreement figure or disagreement rule is reported for the per-reference classification itself (binary ratings were averaged and rounded); D7: the four-way classification is defined in the methods - '(a) fully verifiable, (b) partially correct (real publication with >=1 incorrect detail), (c) unverifiable..., or (d) fully fabricated (DOI resolving to a different publication)' - within a framework 'developed a priori... and remained unmodified', with category distributions reported per model (Supplementary Table S2); D8: both models, all 10 tasks and essay-versus-Q&A strata are reported, in an explicitly exploratory study with no registration or protocol cited.

D1: a single benchmark topic (medical treatment for Peyronie disease from Lee et al, chosen partly because 'we had full information about the interim process and results'), and the prompts were adjusted after outputs were seen - 'we changed the word find to show' after ChatGPT 'did not present studies', and 'we added questions about treatment additionally provided by ChatGPT during the conversation'; D2: the basic prompt format is printed in Textbox 1 ('Could you show RCTs of (A) for Peyronie's disease in (B)?') with prompt-engineering details in Multimedia Appendix 1, ChatGPT's search dates are given ('April 17 to May 6, 2023') and its version as GPT-3.5, but Bing AI's model ('Prometheus', GPT-4-based) and its search dates are given only loosely; D3: ChatGPT questions ran inside continuing conversations arranged in two logical flows (not fresh sessions), 'Each question was repeated at least twice' with answers often changing, and Bing AI was run in the 'Precise' tone under a 20-question session limit - generation settings otherwise unreported for ChatGPT; D4: answers 'evaluated the quality of information based on the title, author, journal, and publication year' against the actual databases and the Lee et al benchmark, and the grade table (Table 1) checks issue, pages, DOI and PMID as well; D5: grading was by the research team ('we evaluated') that also designed and ran the prompts, with no separation or vendor role stated; D6: the paper gives no information on duplicate or blinded grading of answers, or on any agreement figure; D7: the A/B/C/F grade table is defined in the methods with worked examples - A all bibliographic information matched, B essential matched but accessory information mismatched, C essential matched but inappropriate, F title matched only and 'considered as a fake study' - with counts for every grade reported in Table 2; D8: both ChatGPT flows and Bing AI are fully reported in Table 2, but the plug-in method's results (21 of 24 benchmark RCTs provided) appear only in the Discussion with no corresponding counts table, and no registration is cited. Overall high on D1.
